The most immediate threat is energy. Roubini describes the Strait of Hormuz as effectively constrained while the Iran war continues, leaving oil flows vulnerable after crude prices surged earlier this year. Brent jumped another 6% during the week of his comments as the United States and Iran exchanged fresh strikes, while the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve had fallen to a 43-year low the previous month.

Roubini also sees a political clock running toward the U.S. midterm elections. He raised the possibility that President Donald Trump could intensify military pressure on Iran afterward, particularly if Republicans lose the House, turning an already disruptive conflict into a larger geopolitical and inflationary risk. That remains a scenario rather than a prediction, but it is one Roubini thinks markets can't dismiss while the war remains unresolved.

The bond market creates a different constraint on the boom Roubini otherwise likes. Governments need fiscal consolidation, he argues, because persistent deficits can push yields higher and eventually crowd out domestic demand. Yet he also sees some of the increase in real yields as a consequence of the capital-expenditure boom itself, with AI and other industries competing for the same long-term capital governments need to borrow.
That makes higher yields less straightforward than a conventional warning about fiscal collapse.
Strong investment can raise productivity and future economic growth
, but financing extraordinary amounts of new infrastructure also raises the price of capital in the present.
The boom can therefore contribute to one of the financial conditions capable of slowing it down.

Then there are stocks. Roubini thinks a correction can occur without invalidating anything he believes about AI, particularly with yields elevated and markets passing through a historically difficult seasonal stretch. Bank of America calculates that August through October has produced the S&P 500’s weakest average three-month performance since 1928, with an average decline of 7.35% during losing years.
